column1: # The generic word each x86 decode rule carries.
# x86 has no .decode file to write a word on: target/i386 decodes through a
# hand-written table of X86_OP_ENTRY/X86_OP_GROUP rows whose first argument is
# the rule's name.  The name is the key here, and scripts/insn-df-words.py
# turns this file into the X86_DF_WORD_<rule> macros the table expands.  The
# generator reads decode-new.c.inc's own rule names and REFUSES a set that
# does not match this file exactly, in both directions: a rule added to the
# decoder without a word here is a build error, and a row here for a rule the
# decoder does not have is a build error.  So the completeness of this file is
# checked by the build and not by whoever last edited it.
# A word of "-" means the rule has nothing generic to say about itself.  Per
# include/exec/insn-dataflow-words.h that is a statement, not an omission: a
# consumer can tell it apart from a rule that was never reached.  Five rows
# take it, and each says why on its own line.
# The words are adjudications.  Where one differs from what the Capstone-keyed
# classifier published, the reason is in the commit message's enumerated
# classes; the merits, not the incumbency, decide.

column3: dispatcher: gen_3dnow switches on the imm8 suffix byte itself
restores the entire CPU state from SMRAM and transfers control; no one word covers that
raises #UD; a rule with nothing generic to say states no word
dispatcher: 0F 00/01/1A/1B/C7 are four unrelated groups (descriptor-table, MPX, cmpxchg8b/16b, rdrand) and one word would be wrong for three of them
dispatcher: gen_x87 switches on the modrm byte over the whole x87 instruction set
